meta.description: No. Paulo Coelho was first tagged with this line only in 2015. Quote Investigator traces the earliest version to a 1988 book by Fernando Sabino, crediting his father.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Everything will be OK in the end. If it's not OK, it's not the end'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Coelho. The attribution dates only to 2015; the earliest documented version is Fernando Sabino's 1988 book, crediting his father Domingos.

answer.label: Not Paulo Coelho — a misattributed folk saying
answer.authorName: Fernando Sabino (crediting his father, Domingos Sabino)
answer.authorDates: Fernando Sabino, 1923–2004 · Brazilian writer · father Domingos Sabino credited as source
answer.sourceLine: Paulo Coelho is a magnet for feel-good lines he never wrote, and this is one of them. According to Quote Investigator, the saying was pinned on Coelho only in 2015 — years after it was already circulating anonymously. The earliest documented version appears in Brazilian writer Fernando Sabino’s 1988 book O tabuleiro de damas, where Sabino credits the thought to his father, Domingos Sabino. QI names Domingos as the leading candidate while noting he may have been passing along an older adage.

source.heading: What the record shows
source.excerpt: Everything will be OK in the end. If it’s not OK, it’s not the end.
trail: 1988 — earliest documented version. Fernando Sabino’s O tabuleiro de damas gives the saying and credits his father, Domingos Sabino, per Quote Investigator.
2011 — the line goes global. Dev Patel’s character recites a version in The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel, which QI notes helped spread it as an “Indian saying.”

2015 — Coelho enters the story. The line is first attributed to Paulo Coelho in Paul Smith’s book Parenting with a Story, according to Quote Investigator — well after it was already anonymous folk wisdom.
Also wrongly credited to John Lennon (2013) and Oscar Wilde (2017), a classic sign of a floating quotation with no fixed author (QI).
source.excerptNote: The popular English wording is an anonymous paraphrase; Sabino’s 1988 Portuguese line runs closer to “everything works out in the end — if it hasn’t worked out, it’s because it hasn’t reached the end yet.”
source.rightsNote: The exact English wording popularly attributed to Coelho is an anonymous paraphrase with no traced original publication, so no copyright status can be responsibly asserted. The earliest documented form is Fernando Sabino’s 1988 Portuguese text, which would itself be in copyright — but that is a different language and wording, not the line quoted here.

author.name: Fernando Sabino
author.heading: The writer who first put it on the page
author.metaLine: 1923–2004 · Brazilian novelist & journalist · credited the line to his father, Domingos
author.bio: Fernando Sabino was a Brazilian novelist, chronicler and journalist, best known for the 1965 novel O encontro marcado (“A Time to Meet”). In his 1988 book O tabuleiro de damas he set down a version of this saying and attributed it not to himself but to his father, Domingos Sabino — which is why Quote Investigator names Domingos, rather than Fernando or any of the famous later claimants, as the leading candidate for its origin.

misattribution.heading: A quote with many false fathers
misattribution.intro: This is a floating folk saying that has been hung on a series of famous names. None of them wrote it.

items.why: First tied to Coelho only in 2015, via Paul Smith’s Parenting with a Story — years after the line was already circulating anonymously. Quote Investigator finds no evidence Coelho originated it.
A 2013 attribution with no basis in Lennon’s writings or interviews, per QI.
Credited to Wilde by 2017 — the default “famous wit” sink for orphan quotations, again with no source (QI).

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented version is Fernando Sabino’s 1988 book, which credits his father Domingos Sabino — and even QI allows Domingos may have been repeating an older adage (Quote Investigator).

context.heading: Why it floats
lead: The saying’s appeal is exactly why it resists a single author: it is a compact, optimistic tautology that anyone can feel they ‘always knew.’ Once a line reads like folk wisdom, attribution becomes a marketing decision — and a globally famous, aphorism-friendly name like Paulo Coelho is the path of least resistance.

Its modern popularity owes less to any book than to the 2011 film The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel, where it lands as a warm mantra. From there it spread across social media, collecting famous signatures — Lennon, Wilde, Coelho — as it went.
context.pull: A line that sounds like everyone’s wisdom ends up credited to whoever is most quotable.
